newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan insurers to be sidelined at U.S. refunding.
newsitem.headline: Japan insurers to be sidelined at U.S. refunding.

text.p: The major Japanese life insurance companies are not expected to be big players in the U.S. quarterly refunding which begins later on Tuesday, senior fund managers at the firms said on Tuesday.
The institutional investors' appetite at the auction was unlikely to be strong in the first of a three-part refunding effort, particularly before the U.S. presidential election.

Chiyoda Mutual Life Insurance Co, which has been mainly investing its funds in two-year Treasury notes in recent months, said it was not planning to participate in the auction of three-year Treasury notes.
The U.S. Treasury will offer $18.5 billion worth of three-year notes on Tuesday, $10 billion worth of 10-year notes on Wednesday and $10 billion of 30-year bonds on Thursday.

"Looking at the recent coupon levels, it (the three-year note) is not attractive," said Koshi Watanabe, manager of foreign bond investment at Chiyoda. "There is also no reason to participate in the auction before the election."

Watanabe said Chiyoda was willing to wait to see who will hold the balance of power in the U.S. Congress after the election and to see the reaction of the Treasury market before making any further moves.

Some life insurers said they might place bids in Tuesday's auction, depending on the trend of the market right before the auction. However, Japanese investors in general were not keen about investing their funds in longer duration 10-year notes or 30-year bonds.
"We haven't made definite plans at this stage whether to take part in the auction or not," a senior fund manager at a major life insurance firm said.
"We are only waiting to see if the price dips sharply before the auction. But we are not so keen about participating in the auction," the fund manager said.

Japanese life insurers were among leading investers during the Treasury auctions in the late 1980s to early 1990s. Many times during those auctions they purchased 20 percent to 30 percent of the total offering.
Takashi Itoda, manager of the international planning section at Dai-ichi Mutual Life Insurance Co, said Dai-ichi no longer treats U.S. auctions as a special investment occasion.

"We haven't made a final decision, but most probably we'll not bid at the auction. There should be a more appropriate timing in the future rather than bidding before seeing the results of the elections," Itoda said.
